dek: This atlas was built in a fixed order: research first, then graphic interpretation, then the digital object. The method is printed because the limits of the evidence are part of the publication.

levels.name: A fact, practice or object that a cited source records.
levels.text: The source, its date and its limitations are in the bibliography. ‘Documented’ does not mean ‘universal’: a documented practice may be one village’s practice.

levels.name: An argument about what the documentation means.
levels.text: Includes the atlas’s own readings, and the arguments of the scholars cited. Interpretations are attributed where they belong to someone, and marked as editorial where they belong to this edition.

levels.name: A drawing, diagram, sequence or layout made for this atlas.
levels.text: Reconstructions are never presented as historical photographs. Diagrams of ritual sequences, cross types and cemetery plans are analytical drawings, not records of a specific event.

levels.name: A claim carried only as a research lead.
levels.text: The atlas has seen it reported but could not check the source, or the source gives no record. It is kept so that it can be tested, and it is never used to support another claim. A section marked CONTESTED is one where the sources or the scholars cited disagree.

sections.heading: What this atlas is
paras: A collection of research plates ({n} at present) on death in Russian culture, arranged as an atlas rather than as a book: each plate is a composition on one problem, and the index, map and chronology provide routes between them that are not sequential.

The subject is the material and institutional record, not death as a mood: how bodies were handled, how cemeteries were regulated, how the dead were fed and named, how the state counted them, how artists used them.

The plates are issued in four volumes — I, Archæology of Russian Death (A–H, J); II, The Chthonic Landscape (M–R); III, The Unseen (S–V); IV, Memory, Catastrophe and Modernity (I, K, L, W, X) — and the same rules apply to all of them. Plates M–X were written after the first twelve, with fewer images and a smaller body of source reading each; the plate says where it is thin.

sections.heading: What ‘Russian’ means here
paras: It means the tradition of the Russian state and the Russian-language sources, centred on the territory of the Russian Federation and on the imperial and Soviet institutions that shaped it. It does not mean ‘East Slavic’.

Ukrainian, Belarusian and other traditions appear only where a source documents them, and are labelled. The one photographic example from outside the Russian Federation — a commemoration in Ukraine — is on plate D, and the caption says why it is there and what it must not be used to prove.

Several plates lean on material from beside the Russian core: Belarusian-Russian borderland records (plate T), Komi-Permyak recordings, a people who are not Russian (plate U), and Belarusian and Estonian archives behind a comparative study of forest spirits (plate N). Each is labelled in the text as a regional comparison, not as Russian evidence by itself.

sections.heading: Periods, and the refusal of continuity
paras: The atlas distinguishes four rough periods: pre-imperial (to about 1700), imperial (1700–1917), Soviet (1917–1991) and post-Soviet (1991–). These are institutional markers, not a claim that everyone in a period believed the same thing.

The same object can mean different things in different periods, and a practice recorded in 1890 is not evidence for 1490. The chronology marks three caesuras — 1917, the 1930s and 1991 — where the institutions producing the record changed. Continuity is not assumed across them.

sections.heading: Sources, and the refusal of decoration
paras: Priority is given to academic monographs, ethnographic collections, museum and institutional records, and primary texts. Popular websites and press reports appear only where they are the best available account of a specific documented detail, and are marked as such.

A small number of public-domain laments, poems, songs, epitaphs and liturgical texts are printed in full or as marked excerpts, each from the edition named beside it; nothing else is quoted verbatim. A quotation that cannot be checked against a printed text and defended in translation is a decoration, and decoration is the one thing this subject does not need.

Reading depth is stated. Where a source was read only as an abstract, a news excerpt or a machine summary, its bibliography entry and the plate that uses it say so, and the claim is kept at the level that reading can bear.

sections.heading: Geography
paras: The map plots only places for which the atlas has a documentary basis, and it does not shade areas. A photograph of one cemetery is not a distribution; a set of reports gathered from many provinces does not establish a custom’s range.
Where a source gives only a province, the entry says ‘province’. Where a location is approximate, the coordinates are approximate. Two localities lie outside the Russian Federation and are marked.

Several markers stand at a regional centre because the source or photograph names only a region; each entry says so. The three Siberian cities that plate W names (Novosibirsk, Barnaul, Omsk) stand on the map as city markers for an interview’s account; the Urals appear only through two Perm Krai entries.

sections.heading: Language
paras: All visible text is English. Russian terms appear in simplified transliteration — kh, zh, ch, shch, y — with a gloss at first use. The apostrophe marks softness only where it is needed to avoid ambiguity.

All translations from Russian are working translations made for this edition unless a published English translation is named. Dates are given as in the source; no attempt is made to harmonise Old and New Style across the atlas.

sections.heading: The material layer is an argument
paras: The torn edges, toner, halftone screens and photocopy damage in this publication are not a mood laid over the content. They say something about the evidence itself: it gets reproduced, damaged, recopied and is never complete.
The contrast between clean and damaged surfaces is deliberate. Some plates are almost clean because the material they present is confident; others are dense with damage because the record is.

No single overlay is applied to the whole site. Each texture has a role: a dirty photocopy for a print-derived image, paper grain for an editorial page, a halftone screen for a painting that reached most viewers as a reproduction.

sections.heading: What is missing
paras: There is no field survey, no municipal burial register and no systematic study of post-Soviet commercial funerals in this edition. The digital afterlife (plate X) is a survey of claims drawn from abstracts and a news item, not a finding.
The atlas is published with these gaps visible. A reader who wants to extend it should start with the bibliography’s limitation notes: each one says what the source cannot support.

Plates that rest on one interview, one village or one district say so. The Siberian demolitions on plate W are an interviewee’s dated account with no archive cited, and the Moscow reuse of gravestones in the 1930s is carried as unverified.
